Culture · Kochi · Opening day

Kochi made culture a 43-day map.

Japan’s national culture festival opens today. The surprise is not its size, but what the official definition of “culture” allows to stand side by side: yosakoi dance, manga, blades, paper, food and disabled artists.

By Yuji Shimizu · YUJI @ Japan
Published October 25, 2026 at 08:15 JST · 6 min read

At 7:00 this morning, the festival office posted the sentence organizers always hope to publish: today’s opening ceremony will go ahead as planned. With that short notice, Kochi became the center of Japan’s largest national cultural gathering for the next 43 days.

The 41st National Cultural Festival and the 26th National Arts and Culture Festival for Persons with Disabilities run together from October 25 through December 6. Kochi has never hosted the combined event before. The calendar spreads across the prefecture rather than concentrating culture inside one museum or theater.

43days from opening to close
41stNational Cultural Festival
2017year the disability arts festival was integrated

The official theme translates roughly as “Hearts dance, culture blooms.” That may sound ceremonial until the event list supplies its verbs: dance, draw, cut, fold, cook, sing, watch, discuss and travel. Kochi is presenting culture as something people do, not a shelf of treasures preserved behind glass.

The most revealing feature is administrative: since 2017, the national festival has been integrated with the country’s arts and culture festival for disabled people. Inclusion is not a parallel weekend. It is part of the same 43-day map.

Why Kochi can hold these worlds together

Kochi occupies the southern side of Shikoku, facing the Pacific while the Shikoku Mountains define its inland edge. Its long coast changes character from ria in the west to raised shoreline and broad beaches in the east. Warm rain, typhoons, rivers and forests have shaped both livelihoods and a strong regional identity.

The festival office names food from sea, mountain and river; Tosa washi paper; Tosa forged blades; manga; and yosakoi among the prefecture’s signatures. None began as the same kind of object. Washi is material, a blade is a tool, manga is reproducible media, and yosakoi is a moving crowd. The festival treats all four as ways a place transmits knowledge.

Yosakoi makes the strongest visual bridge. The Kochi festival began in 1954 as a postwar effort to revive the city. Teams now build performances from synchronized movement, music, costumes and wooden clappers called naruko. The format travelled widely because it could preserve a recognizable rule while allowing each team to redesign everything around it.

Manga offers a different kind of export. Kochi is associated with creators including Anpanman author Takashi Yanase, while the prefecture has cultivated manga competitions and museum culture. An official festival that places manga beside traditional craft does not need to argue that one is serious and the other popular. Both record how images move between generations.

Official Yosakoi Kochi Culture Festival 2026 video from the prefectural organizing committee. It shows the actual host culture and festival program.

Forty-three days change the way a visitor looks

A one-day festival asks a visitor to choose a stage. A 43-day festival asks them to choose a route. The official program highlights media-arts exhibitions, an immersive museum, performing arts and local cultural programs. Some events began before opening day, while the national festival period supplies the shared frame through December 6.

That extended period matters outside Kochi City. A visitor can connect the prefectural capital with coastal and mountain municipalities, seeing how a craft or dance changes with geography. The cultural agency’s definition explicitly links the arts with tourism, education, welfare, industry, international exchange and town planning. The festival is therefore both performance and regional policy.

The opening ceremony gives that policy a single television image; the weeks afterward reveal whether the map truly distributes attention. Small venues need usable travel information, accessible entrances and schedules clear enough for visitors who do not read Japanese fluently. Cultural inclusion can fail at a staircase or an unclear ticket page long before an artwork is reached.

A national festival with a local accent

Japan’s National Cultural Festival began in 1986. Emperor Naruhito and Empress Masako attend under a tradition that began when the current emperor, then Crown Prince, participated in the first event. Each host prefecture inherits the national format, but the content changes with local artists, landscapes and institutions.

Kochi’s accent is useful precisely because it resists the usual overseas shorthand for Japanese culture. There is no need to choose between “ancient tradition” and “modern pop.” A sheet of handmade paper, a manga panel and a dance team crossing an avenue all depend on trained hands, shared rules and an audience that recognizes the form.

That does not make them interchangeable. Tosa washi depends on fibers, water and papermaking knowledge; Tosa blades carry histories of agriculture, forestry and metalwork; manga depends on publishing and reproduction; yosakoi exists through bodies occupying public space. Putting them on one calendar should sharpen those differences, not flatten them into a generic Japan brand.

What to watch after the ceremony

The official site will update event status and weather changes throughout the run. Visitors should confirm venue-specific tickets and access before travelling; the opening ceremony itself was reaffirmed only at 7:00 a.m. today because weather can change plans.

The deeper measure will come after December 6. Did disabled artists gain durable audiences rather than ceremonial visibility? Did visitors reach municipalities beyond the capital? Did local children see their own practices as creative futures rather than relics? Those outcomes are harder to count than attendance, but they explain why a national festival lasts more than one weekend.

For an overseas reader, Kochi’s 43-day map offers a better question than “What is traditional Japan?” Ask instead who is keeping a practice alive, what materials and spaces it needs, and how a form changes when new people enter it. Culture blooms because someone keeps doing the work.
